blocks.text: A workshop's induction motors draw 40 A from the mains but deliver only as much useful work as 30 A of purely resistive load would. The utility still has to supply the extra 10 A, and bills the workshop for it. The difference comes from impedance: in AC circuits, inductors and capacitors push current out of step with voltage, and that changes how power is counted.

blocks.markdown: In sinusoidal steady state every element obeys a generalised Ohm's law with complex numbers. The **impedance** $Z$ (ohm) relates the voltage and current phasors, $\mathbf V=Z\,\mathbf I$. A resistor has $Z_R=R$; an inductor has $Z_L=j\omega L$; a capacitor has $Z_C=1/(j\omega C)=-j/(\omega C)$, where $\omega=2\pi f$ is the angular frequency in rad/s and $j=\sqrt{-1}$. The imaginary part is the **reactance** $X$ (ohm): inductive reactance $X_L=\omega L$ and capacitive reactance $X_C=1/(\omega C)$.

blocks.title: Series RLC impedance
blocks.text: Impedances in series add. $Z=R+j\omega L+\dfrac{1}{j\omega C}=R+jX$, with net reactance $X=\omega L-1/(\omega C)$. Its magnitude is $|Z|=\sqrt{R^2+X^2}$ and its phase is $\varphi=\arctan(X/R)$; the current lags the voltage by $\varphi$ when $X>0$ (inductive) and leads when $X<0$ (capacitive).

blocks.caption: Series RLC impedance at angular frequency omega

blocks.title: Impedance at a given frequency
blocks.prompt: A series circuit has $R=47\ \Omega$, $L=20$ mH and $C=22$ uF, driven at $f=100$ Hz. Find the net reactance, the magnitude of the impedance and the phase angle.
blocks.answer: |Z| = 76.0 ohm at -51.8 degrees: the circuit is capacitive at 100 Hz, so the current leads the voltage.

blocks.markdown: **Resonance.** $X_L$ grows with frequency and $X_C$ falls with it. At the **resonant frequency** $f_0$ they are equal, the reactances cancel, and $Z=R$ is purely resistive and at its minimum. The current for a given source voltage is then at its maximum, $V/R$. Below $f_0$ the circuit is capacitive; above it, inductive.

**AC power.** For a load with voltage $V$ and current $I$ (both rms) and phase difference $\varphi$ between them, three powers are defined. **Real (active) power** $P=VI\cos\varphi$ in watts does useful work and heats the load. **Reactive power** $Q=VI\sin\varphi$ in volt-amperes reactive (var) is exchanged back and forth with the stored fields and does no net work. **Apparent power** $S=VI$ in volt-amperes (VA) is what the supply must carry. They form a right-angled triangle, and the **power factor** is $\mathrm{pf}=\cos\varphi=P/S$.

blocks.title: Power of an AC load
blocks.prompt: A load draws 5.0 A rms from a 230 V rms supply with the current lagging the voltage by 30 degrees. Find $S$, $P$, $Q$ and the power factor.

steps.text: Power factor, lagging because the load is inductive.

blocks.answer: S = 1150 VA, P = 996 W, Q = 575 var, pf = 0.866 lagging.

items: Only the resistance dissipates real power: $P=I^2R$.
A low power factor means more current for the same real power, so larger cables and losses.
Reactive power does no net work but loads the supply.
At resonance the voltages across $L$ and $C$ cancel at the series ends but each can be larger than the source voltage.

blocks.title: Why power factor matters
blocks.text: For a fixed $P$ and $V$, the current is $I=P/(V\,\mathrm{pf})$. Halving the power factor doubles the current and quadruples the $I^2R$ loss in the supply cables, so utilities penalise low power factor.

points: Series impedance $Z=R+j(\omega L-1/\omega C)$; magnitude $\sqrt{R^2+X^2}$, phase $\arctan(X/R)$.

questions.stem: A load draws 10 A at 230 V rms and consumes 1.15 kW of real power. What is its power factor?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: pf = 1 would require P = 2300 W.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: 0.87 is cos 30 degrees, unrelated to these numbers.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: pf cannot exceed 1; this inverts the ratio.

questions.explanation: Apparent power is $S=VI=230\times10=2300$ VA, so $\mathrm{pf}=P/S=1150/2300=0.50$. The power factor is always between 0 and 1.

questions.stem: A series RLC circuit is driven below its resonant frequency. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The net reactance is capacitive and the current leads the voltage
The net reactance is inductive and the current lags the voltage
The impedance is at its maximum

questions.correctOptionText: The net reactance is capacitive and the current leads the voltage

distractorRationale.a: Correct: below f_0, X_C > X_L so X is negative.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: that describes frequencies above f_0.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: the impedance is at its minimum (R) at resonance, and rises either side.

questions.explanation: At low frequency $X_C=1/\omega C$ is large and $X_L=\omega L$ is small, so the net reactance $X<0$. A negative reactance means the current leads the voltage.

questions.stem: A load takes 400 W of real power and 500 VA of apparent power. What is its reactive power?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this subtracts S - P instead of using the triangle.

questions.explanation: The power triangle gives $S^2=P^2+Q^2$, so $Q=\sqrt{500^2-400^2}=300$ var. Powers do not add or subtract linearly.

questions.stem: A series circuit has $R=68\ \Omega$, $L=50$ mH and $C=47$ uF, driven at 60 Hz. What is the magnitude of the impedance, in ohms?
A series RLC tuned circuit uses $L=2.2$ mH and $C=4.7$ uF. What is its resonant frequency, in hertz?
A 230 V, 50 Hz motor draws 1.80 kW of real power at a power factor of 0.75 lagging. What is its reactive power, in var?
questions.explanation: The apparent power is $S=P/\mathrm{pf}=1800/0.75=2400$ VA. Then $Q=\sqrt{S^2-P^2}=\sqrt{2400^2-1800^2}=1587$ var (inductive).

questions.stem: Describe what happens to the impedance, the current amplitude and the phase of a series RLC circuit as the source frequency is swept upward through resonance, for a fixed source voltage. Explain why the impedance is minimum at resonance.
markingGuide: X_L = omega L increases with frequency and X_C = 1/(omega C) decreases
Below f_0 the net reactance is capacitive (negative), above f_0 inductive (positive)
At f_0, X_L = X_C so reactances cancel and Z = R (purely resistive, minimum |Z|)
Current amplitude V/|Z| therefore peaks at resonance at V/R
Phase of current relative to voltage goes from leading to zero to lagging
questions.explanation: As $f$ rises, $X_L=\omega L$ grows and $X_C=1/\omega C$ shrinks. Below $f_0$ the net reactance is negative (capacitive), at $f_0$ the two cancel so $Z=R$ and $|Z|$ is minimum, and above $f_0$ it is positive (inductive). The current amplitude $V/|Z|$ peaks at resonance and the phase moves from leading to zero to lagging.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kW single-phase load is supplied at 230 V rms. Compare the supply current when its power factor is 1.0 and when it is 0.60. Explain what this means for cable losses and why a utility prefers a high power factor.
markingGuide: Cable loss I^2 R scales with the square of the current: ratio (1/0.6)^2 = 2.8 times
Reactive power does no work but needs current, so low pf wastes capacity and increases losses
questions.explanation: Since $P=VI\,\mathrm{pf}$, the current is $I=P/(V\,\mathrm{pf})$: 8.7 A at unity pf and 14.5 A at pf 0.60. The $I^2R$ loss in the supply cables rises by $(1/0.6)^2\approx2.8$ times for the same useful power. The extra current only carries reactive power, which does no work but occupies cable and transformer capacity.
